or_r_i_p_the.blurb: A short, steep panel of tuff in the Lookout Point cluster of crags in the Willamette Valley, roughly half an hour by road from Eugene. Fourteen lines in total: twelve sport routes running from 5.11 up into 5.14, plus a couple of boulder problems around V13. The wall is only 20 to 40 feet tall, but it overhangs, and the climbing is about hard pulls between small one and two finger pockets. It faces northeast and sits in shade nearly all day, which keeps it climbable in conditions that shut other crags. Holds can be fragile when damp. This is a place for strong climbers, not a warm-up venue.

or_hidden_wall_2.blurb: A south-facing wall tucked into Hidden Valley, one of the side drainages of Burnt River Canyon in northeast Oregon. All fourteen routes are bolted sport lines, split across three sectors: an easy low-angle slab on the upper left, a taller corner in the middle that begins on a ramp and steepens, and a lower right section with longer lines up the centre and shorter ones either side. Grades run from 5.7 to 5.11, with the bulk around 5.9 to 5.10, so it suits a mixed group. A 70 m rope helps on the longest lines. The canyon is hot in summer and quiet year round.

or_3_long_wall.blurb: A band of welded tuff cliff along the trail at Rattlesnake, a bolted sport crag in the hills above the Rogue Valley near Medford. Thirteen sport routes, roughly 50 to 60 feet tall, graded from 5.11 to 5.13, most of them in the 5.11 and low 5.12 range. The left portion has the more consistent rock; the steeper, harder right end is looser and a helmet is a good idea there. Rock quality at Rattlesnake can swing from solid to crumbly within a single pitch, so check holds. Spring and fall are the comfortable seasons here.

or_11_emerald_city.blurb: A sport wall within Terra Nova, the bolted cliff zone near Shady Cove in southwest Oregon. Thirteen sport routes ranging from 5.8 to 5.12, but the real concentration is 5.10 and 5.11, so it works for climbers who have moved beyond the easy grades without being a hard-only venue. The routes lie on a left wall and a right wall inside a gully reached by walking downhill to a large log and heading left. Brush grows thickly in the gully, which is the main complaint. Helmets and a stick clip are worth bringing to Terra Nova generally.

or_i_the_fourth_horseman.blurb: A cluster of towers at Smith Rock, in the stretch between Morning Glory Wall and the Dihedrals. At a glance the formation looks like a pile of crumbling rock, yet it holds a good set of moderate lines. Thirteen routes in all: seven sport and six trad, from about 5.7 to 5.12, with the weight at 5.10. The trad side is mostly crack climbing, including a few two-pitch lines, while the sport routes are single pitch. It is a handy choice for someone who wants cracks at an approachable grade and a break from the busier faces nearby.

or_4_big_ben_tower.blurb: A tower in the Monument Area, the quieter, more remote corner of Smith Rock State Park. The face looks almost directly south, so it collects sun for most of the day and is a reasonable pick when it is cool. Thirteen routes, ten sport and three trad, from 5.10 up to 5.13, concentrated at 5.12. Expect to have it largely to yourself. Some holds are creaky, so test before you trust, and a couple of lines run all the way to the summit while others stay near the base.

or_d_maiden_oregon_wall.blurb: A steep buttress of salmon-coloured rock on the Marsupial Wall, across the gorge from the main Smith Rock cliffs. It rises above a small cave and offers big features and solid stone, with a view toward the Cascades. Thirteen sport routes: a single easy slab line, then everything from 5.10 up to 5.13, centred on 5.11 and 5.12. In winter the sun reaches it around midday; in summer the morning stays shaded until the early afternoon. Plan on about an hour of walking to get there, and expect very little company.

or_gym_wall.blurb: An open, steep slab on the left side of West Gully at Scorpion Buttress, part of the Callahans climbing area west of Roseburg. Routes are bolted close together in the style of an indoor wall, which makes it a good place to practise footwork. Thirteen climbs: eleven sport, one trad and one aid line, with grades from 5.7 to 5.11 and most of them between 5.7 and 5.10. You get in by rappelling from the butte top or by a steep switchback trail down to the middle of the gully, where there is room to set out pads.

_conflicts.or_hidden_wall_2: Stored rock is phyllite; https://mountainproject.com/area/106548526/burnt-river-canyon calls the Burnt River Canyon crags limestone (geologically marble). Blurb names no rock.
_conflicts.or_gym_wall: Stored rock is mudstone; https://www.mountainproject.com/area/200927241/scorpion-buttress and https://www.mountainproject.com/area/106279271/the-callahans both say Tyee sandstone. Blurb names no rock.
